claims.text: The proposed approach combines enhanced-sampling molecular dynamics, thermodynamic integration, and machine-learning interatomic potentials calibrated at high temperatures.
The approach can accurately predict melting temperatures across a broad range of high-entropy-alloy compositions.
The approach can accurately predict enthalpies and entropies of fusion for high-entropy alloys.
The approach can accurately predict volume changes at melting and liquid-phase free energies for high-entropy alloys.
Refractory NbMoTaW-related high-entropy alloys are relevant examples of single-phase BCC initial systems.
Refractory high-entropy alloys have high melting temperatures that create processing difficulties for traditional techniques.
The simulation framework explicitly resolves configurational entropy, interfacial energies, and bulk free energies during the solid-to-liquid transition.
Combining advanced free-energy sampling with machine-learned potentials captures the energetic contributions of all constituent elements.
Capturing element-specific energetic contributions overcomes limitations of compositional averaging techniques.
The proposed computational method overcomes limitations of traditional calorimetric methods.
Predicted melting properties will agree with experimental measurements to within approximately 5–10%.
The proposed method will be more accurate and efficient than conventional approaches.
Conventional calorimetry and averaged computational models often provide insufficient resolution for complex phase behavior in multicomponent HEAs.
The approach is expected to be robust for refractory, single-phase BCC high-entropy alloys.
The approach may be limited for compositions exhibiting substantial multiphase behavior or nonequilibrium solidification.
Differences in constituent melting temperatures can affect elemental distribution during solidification in refractory HEAs.
Scalability of the approach across the full HEA composition space has not been validated.
A deviation greater than approximately 10% for any specified thermodynamic parameter under defined equilibrium conditions would rule out the proposed approach.
